newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada-U.S. grain producers to review trade report.
newsitem.headline: Canada-U.S. grain producers to review trade report.

text.p: Canadian and U.S. grain producer groups agreed to meet in Seattle June 14 to review the suggestions of a 1995 binational trade panel that were not implemented, an Alberta Barley Commission (ABC) official said.

"The Canada-U.S. Joint Commission report on the grain trade made pretty constructive recommendations but it was pretty much ignored by (then Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph) Goodale," ABC general manager Clif Foster said.
Goodale was re-elected in his Saskatchewan riding of Wascana on Monday but it was not clear whether he'd be reappointed to the agriculture portfolio next Wednesday.
The commission recommended in 1995 a producer-industry committee to deal with short-term cross border issues.
North Dakota farmers complained to U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky in April about Canadian wheat and barley shipments into the United States.

The U.S. would like to limit Canadian grain imports at 1.5 million tonnes in the current marketing year ending September 12, as it did for Canadian wheat and durum imports in 1995 under trade law that is no longer valid under World Trade Organization rules. Canada opposes any cap on grain exports.
The commission also suggested both nations agree on a common method of assessing grain quality and drop the requirement for end-use certificates.
It recommended both countries address "trade distorting" factors such as the U.S. Export Enhancement Program and the Canadian Wheat Board.
"I am hopefull that we'll be able to answer those questions on cross border trade at the end of the meeting in Seattle," Foster said.

Goodale campaigned in Wascana on a promise to reintroduce amendments to the CWB Act that would revamp the state agency's corporate structure and allow it to buy up to a quarter of Prairie wheat output on the spot market while preserving its monopoly seller status.
